claims.source: Besides speed.moving: (t(3) = 0.096, p=0.929), photoinhibition in ArchT3.0 OnTarget_antPAG mice consistently changed locomotor parameters in a direction opposite to the ChR2 mice (Figure 3a–h): Distance moved (t(3) = –3.176, p=0.050, g = –0.832 [large]), time in immobile state: (t(3) = 5.369, p=0.013, g = –1.712 [large]), time in center (t(3) = –4.590, p=0.019, g = –0.885 [large]) and time in periphery (t(3) = 1.367, p=0.265).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of optogenetic inhibition experiments with reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: The large volume of virus injected (200 nl) and the highly penetrant and strongly expressing viral serotype of the vector used (AAV5) led to expression of ChR2 not only in the parvafoxFoxb1 neurons but also in other Foxb1-expressing hypothalamic neurons in the neighboring mammillary region.
claims.source: A comment about the specificity of the optogenetic results: the large volume of virus injected (200 nl) and the highly penetrant and strongly expressing viral serotype of the vector used (AAV5) led to expression of ChR2 not only (as intended) in the parvafoxFoxb1 neurons but also in other Foxb1-expressing hypothalamic neurons in the neighboring mammillary region.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a technical limitation in the experimental design.

claims.claim: Of all the mammillary nuclei only the dorsal premammillary nuclei (PMd) send axons to the rostral dlPAG.
claims.source: However, of all the mammillary nuclei only the dorsal premammillary nuclei (PMd) send axons to the rostral dlPAG (Vertes, 1992; Meller and Dennis, 1986; Canteras and Swanson, 1992), where the tip of the glass fibers for the optogenetic activation were implanted.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: In the optogenetic experiments, the terminals from the PMdFoxb1 were co-activated with those of the parvafoxFoxb1.
claims.source: In our experiments, the terminals from the PMdFoxb1 were therefore co-activated with those of the parvafoxFoxb1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity and the experimental design.

claims.claim: Projections to the rostral dlPAG from other mamillary neurons are very scarce.
claims.source: Projections to the rostral dlPAG from other mamillary neurons are very scarce (Allen and Hopkins, 1990; Shen, 1983; Beart et al., 1990; Cruce, 1977; Canteras et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals originating from the hypothalamic parvafox nucleus and/or PMd and projecting to the anterior PAG induces a state of immobility and hypoactivity.
claims.source: In summary, optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals originating from the hypothalamic parvafox nucleus and/or PMd and projecting to the anterior PAG induces a state of immobility and hypoactivity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the optogenetic experimental data.

claims.claim: Stimulation at more posterior positions along the PAG and/or ventral to the dlPAG columns are inefficient in inducing immobility behavior.
claims.source: Stimulation at more posterior positions along the PAG and/or ventral to the dlPAG columns are inefficient in inducing this behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from optogenetic experiments comparing different stimulation sites.

claims.claim: The observed effect of optogenetic activation is bidirectional, in the sense that inhibition of the same terminals in the anterior PAG induces increased distance moved, and time spent in the center of the arena, while decreasing the time spent in an immobile state.
claims.source: The observed effect is bidirectional, in the sense that inhibition of the same terminals in the anterior PAG induces increased distance moved, and time spent in the center of the arena, while decreasing the time spent in an immobile state.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the bidirectional effects observed with activation vs. inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: A cholecystokinin (Cck)-expressing population of neurons in the PMd has been shown to induce escape behavior in mice.
claims.source: In contrast to this finding, a cholecystokinin (Cck)-expressing population of neurons in the PMd has been shown to induce escape behavior in mice (Wang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Wang et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The Cck-expressing and the Foxb1-expressing PMd neurons are distinct, separate neuronal groups regulating opposite behaviors.
claims.source: We hypothesized that the Cck-expressing and the Foxb1-expressing PMd neurons are distinct, separate neuronal groups regulating opposite behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on their observations.

claims.claim: K-nearest neighbor clustering resulted in 24 distinct cell types detected in the ventral-posterior hypothalamus.
claims.source: After quality control, normalization, and integration of all four datasets (from two female and two male mice), k-nearest neighbor clustering resulted in 24 distinct cell types detected in the ventral-posterior hypothalamus (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis with reference to Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Cluster 9 was identified as the PMd based on expression of PMd markers.
claims.source: Plotting the expression levels of a set of PMd markers identified by Mickelsen et al. (i.e. Cck, Foxb1, Synpr, Dlk1, Ebf3, and Stxbp6) onto the UMAP plot identified cluster 9 as the PMd (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 4b.

claims.claim: There are significantly higher expression levels of Cck than Foxb1 in the PMd cluster.
claims.source: Plotting gene expression with fixed scales across both genes reveals significantly higher expression levels of Cck than Foxb1 in the PMd cluster (column d1 in Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 4d.

claims.claim: Simultaneous visualization of both Cck and Foxb1 expression levels within the PMd cluster shows a biased expression pattern of Cck- and Foxb1-expressing cells towards opposing sides of the PMd cluster.
claims.source: Simultaneous visualization of both Cck and Foxb1 expression levels within the PMd cluster shows a biased expression pattern of Cck- and Foxb1-expressing cells towards opposing sides of the PMd cluster (column d2 in Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression visualization with reference to Figure 4d.

claims.claim: There is a substantial number of single-positive cells for each of Cck and Foxb1 in the PMd cluster.
claims.source: There is a substantial number of single-positive cells for each of the two genes (column d3 in Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 4d.

claims.claim: There is a group of PMd neurons co-expressing both Cck and Foxb1, but very few of them show high expression levels of both genes.
claims.source: There is indeed a group of PMd neurons co-expressing both markers, but very few of them show high expression levels of both genes.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: Although both Cck and Foxb1 are expressed throughout the entire PMd cluster, there are two well-defined, distinct, subpopulations of neurons expressing either Cck or Foxb1 but not both.
claims.source: In summary, although both Cck and Foxb1 are expressed throughout the entire PMd cluster, there are two well-defined, distinct, subpopulations of neurons expressing either Cck or Foxb1 but not both.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: The PMdFoxb1 is a novel subdivision of the PMd with functional distinction from the PMdCck.
claims.source: We were hence able to introduce the presence of the PMdFoxb1 as a novel subdivision of the PMd with functional distinction from the PMdCck.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical, functional, and transcriptomic data.

claims.claim: Two studies had previously identified the parvalbumin+ subpopulation of the parvafox nucleus (parvafoxPvalb) to be involved in nociceptive behaviors.
claims.source: Two studies had previously identified the parvalbumin+ subpopulation of the parvafox nucleus (parvafoxPvalb) to be involved in nociceptive behaviors (Roccaro-Waldmeyer et al., 2018; Siemian et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: No significant difference was observed between BL and Stim conditions in any of the three tested animal groups in hot plate experiments.
claims.source: In these experiments, we did not observe any significant difference between BL and Stim conditions in any of the three tested animal groups (Figure 5, ChR2-OnTarget_antPAG: Number of shakes before endpoint t(5) = –0.442, p=0.677 and latency until endpoint t(5) = 0.515, p=0.629; ChR-OffTarget: Number of shakes before endpoint t(10) = –1.076, p=0.307 and latency until endpoint t(10) = 1.716, p=0.117; ArchT3.0-OnTarget_antPAG: Number of shakes before endpoint t(5) = –0.344, p=0.753 and latency until endpoint z=1.150, p=0.875; all reported results are from Welch's t tests, except the last result that was obtained by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test due to non-normality of the data).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of hot plate test data with reference to Figure 5.

claims.claim: The parvafoxFoxb1 does not exert a reciprocal effect on the parvafoxPvalb's role in pain sensation.
claims.source: These results reveal that the parvafoxFoxb1 does not excert a reciprocal effect on the parvafoxPvalb's role in pain sensation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hot plate test results.

claims.claim: The absence of altered latencies until endpoint behavior demonstrates that the immobility phenotype of ChR2-expressing Foxb1-Cre mice can be escaped when thermal stimulus intensity reaches nociceptive threshold.
claims.source: Interestingly though, the absence of altered latencies until endpoint behavior demonstrates that the immobility phenotype of ChR2-expressing Foxb1-Cre mice can be escaped, when thermal stimulus intensity reaches nociceptive threshold (Figure 5a).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the hot plate test results with reference to Figure 5a.

claims.claim: A sudden onset of bradycardia was observed in three mice immediately after starting the optogenetic activation.
claims.source: The measurement of cardiovascular parameters in a group of 8 Foxb1-Cre mice revealed a sudden onset of bradycardia in three mice (106/21–10, 34/21–7, 34/21–10), immediately after starting the optogenetic activation (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from cardiovascular telemetry experiments with reference to Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The heart rate (HR) decreased abruptly by 30–60 beats/min but could reach 290 beats/min in some experiments.
claims.source: The heart rate (HR) decreased abruptly by 30–60 beats/min but could reach 290 beats/min in some experiments (Figure 6b; 106/21–10).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from cardiovascular telemetry experiments with reference to Figure 6b.

claims.claim: The light-induced cardiovascular responses had an on-kinetic of 1–10 s and at light offset, the HR returned to the baseline levels nearly instantaneously.
claims.source: The light-induced cardiovascular responses had an on-kinetic of 1–10 s and at light offset, the HR returned to the baseline levels nearly instantaneously.
claims.evidence: This is a temporal observation from cardiovascular telemetry experiments.

claims.claim: Augmenting the light intensity of the stimulation increased the extent of HR deceleration.
claims.source: Augmenting the light intensity of the stimulation increased the extent of HR deceleration.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from cardiovascular telemetry experiments with varying stimulation intensity.

claims.claim: In the three mice showing bradycardia, the glass fibers were located bilaterally over the rostral part of the dlPAG.
claims.source: In these three mice, the glass fibers were located bilaterally over the rostral part of the dlPAG (Figure 7a and b).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical observation from histological verification with reference to Figure 7.

claims.claim: Glass fibers located over the Su3 or over the intermediate or caudal dlPAG or the PV2 nucleus did not trigger cardiovascular reactions.
claims.source: Glass fibers located over the Su3 or over the intermediate or caudal dlPAG or the PV2 nucleus did not trigger cardiovascular reactions.
claims.evidence: This is a negative observation from cardiovascular telemetry experiments with different fiber placements.

claims.claim: In the five Pvalb-Cre mice with similar injection of Chr2 in the parvafoxPvalb and glass fibers positioned bilaterally over the rostral dlPAG, no changes in cardiovascular parameters were measured.
claims.source: In the five Pvalb-Cre mice with similar injection of Chr2 in the parvafoxPvalb and glass fibers positioned bilaterally over the rostral dlPAG, no changes in cardiovascular parameters were measured.
claims.evidence: This is a negative observation from control experiments using a different Cre line.

claims.claim: In mouse 106-21/10, the HRV changed from 80ms during the baseline period to 120ms during the optogenetic stimulation.
claims.source: In mouse 106-21/10 (Supplementary file 5), the HRV changed from 80ms during the baseline period to 120ms during the optogenetic stimulation the STDEV of cycle duration changed from 3.8 ms to 20.6ms [+445%].
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from heart rate variability analysis.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ cell bodies in the PMd and parvafox nuclei of the hypothalamus, as well as optogenetic excitation of their axonal endings in the dlPAG both lead to a phenotypic presentation congruent with the reaction observed during innate defensive behavior: tachypnea, immobility, and bradycardia.
claims.source: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ cell bodies in the PMd and parvafox nuclei of the hypothalamus, as well as optogenetic excitation of their axonal endings in the dlPAG both lead to a phenotypic presentation congruent with the reaction observed during innate defensive behavior: tachypnea, immobility, and bradycardia.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings from the study.

claims.claim: Injection of both DREADD ligands (CNO and clozapine) reproducibly led to the same phenotype in DREADD-expressing animals but not in control animals.
claims.source: We have shown that injection of both DREADD ligands reproducibly led to the same phenotype in DREADD-expressing animals but not in control animals.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the DREADD experimental results.

claims.claim: The effect of increased respiratory effort is at least partly mediated by the projections of the parvafoxFoxb1 neurons to the dlPAG.
claims.source: We infer that this effect is at least partly mediated by the projections of the parvafoxFoxb1 neurons to the dlPAG.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity and functional results.

claims.claim: Injections of excitatory aminoacids D,L-hopmocysteic acid (DLH) in the dlPAG raise respiratory activity by an increase in respiratory rate.
claims.source: In accordance with this assumption, injections of excitatory aminoacids D,L-hopmocysteic acid (DLH) in the dlPAG raise respiratory activity by an increase in respiratory rate (Iigaya et al., 2010; Subramanian and Holstege, 2014; Dampney et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Immobility is the absence of movements associated with an increase in respiration and muscle tone.
claims.source: Immobility is the absence of movements associated with an increase in respiration and muscle tone (Fanselow, 1994; Kalin and Shelton, 1989) and is consistently correlated with heart rate deceleration (Vianna and Carrive, 2005; Walker and Carrive, 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work defining immobility.

claims.claim: Immobility is consistently correlated with heart rate deceleration.
claims.source: Immobility is the absence of movements associated with an increase in respiration and muscle tone (Fanselow, 1994; Kalin and Shelton, 1989) and is consistently correlated with heart rate deceleration (Vianna and Carrive, 2005; Walker and Carrive, 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The body immobility observed in the open field test perturbed the execution and therefore may have influenced the results of the hot-plate test.
claims.source: The body immobility observed in the open field test perturbed the execution and therefore may have influenced the results of the hot-plate test.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about a potential confound in the hot plate experiments.

claims.claim: The PMd and the parvafoxFoxb1 originate from the same Foxb1+ cell lineage have differential connectivity pattern and as a result they may assume distinct functional tasks.
claims.source: The PMd and the parvafoxFoxb1 originate from the same Foxb1+ cell lineage have differential connectivity pattern and as a result they may assume distinct functional tasks (Bilella et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The PMd receives afferences from the infralimbic and prelimbic areas of the medial frontal cortex.

results.result: Foxb1-expressing neurons are located in the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) and parvafox nucleus of the lateral hypothalamus, with projections terminating in the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (dlPAG). These anatomical features are established through developmental lineage tracing and prior anatomical studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C7-C10 establish the anatomical organization of Foxb1+ neurons through citations to established literature (Alvarez-Bolado et al., 2000; Canteras and Swanson, 1992; Bilella et al., 2016). These are well-documented anatomical facts that provide the foundation for the functional experiments.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ neurons using hM3Dq with clozapine or CNO increases respiratory rate (BPM) by selectively shortening inspiratory time through increased peak inspiratory flow, without altering tidal volume. This effect is specific to hM3Dq-expressing animals and not observed in control or hM4Di groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C34 provide comprehensive statistical evidence from whole-body plethysmography with appropriate controls (DREADD_neg, hM4Di), multiple ligands (clozapine, CNO), and c-Fos validation. The mixed-design ANOVA with post-hoc tests and effect size calculations support the respiratory phenotype. The specificity is confirmed by lack of effects in controls.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ neurons produces only small or negligible effects on locomotor activity that are unlikely to explain the large respiratory changes observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 demonstrate that while some statistically significant effects on locomotion were observed, the effect sizes were small (g=0.225) or negligible (g=0.081), contrasting with the large effect sizes for respiratory parameters. This appropriately addresses potential confounds and strengthens the respiratory findings.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals in the rostral dlPAG induces immobility with short latency, characterized by decreased distance moved, reduced speed, increased time immobile, and altered spatial distribution. The effect is anatomically specific to the rostral dlPAG and shows dose-dependency.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C52, C58-C59 provide quantitative behavioral data with appropriate statistics (Welch's t-tests, large effect sizes g>1.0) and anatomical specificity (OnTarget vs OffTarget groups). The behavioral phenotype is well-characterized across multiple parameters with consistent directionality. Videos provide qualitative validation.

results.result: Optogenetic inhibition using ArchT3.0 produces bidirectional effects opposite to ChR2 activation, supporting the specificity of the projection and arguing against antidromic propagation artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C60, C137-C140 demonstrate bidirectional control with ArchT3.0 producing opposite effects to ChR2. This is critical for establishing causality and ruling out technical artifacts. The logic regarding antidromic propagation (C140) is sound, and the use of inhibitory opsins circumvents backpropagation concerns (C137).

results.result: The optogenetic experiments co-activate both parvafoxFoxb1 and PMdFoxb1 terminals in the dlPAG due to viral spread, though only PMd among mammillary nuclei projects to rostral dlPAG.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 acknowledge an important technical limitation with appropriate citations (Vertes, 1992; Canteras and Swanson, 1992). The authors correctly identify that viral spread affects interpretation but provide anatomical evidence that only PMd among mammillary nuclei projects to the stimulation site. This transparency is important for interpretation.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that the PMd contains distinct subpopulations of Cck+ and Foxb1+ neurons with biased spatial distribution, establishing PMdFoxb1 as a novel functional subdivision distinct from PMdCck.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70 provide computational analysis of published scRNA-seq data with appropriate clustering, marker validation, and visualization. The identification of single-positive populations for Cck and Foxb1 with spatial segregation supports the existence of distinct subpopulations. The analysis is methodologically sound with proper quality control and validation against Allen Brain Atlas.

results.result: Optogenetic manipulation of Foxb1+ terminals does not affect thermal nociception in hot plate tests, though the immobility phenotype can be overcome by nociceptive stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 show no significant differences in hot plate responses across groups with appropriate statistical tests. The interpretation that immobility can be escaped with sufficient stimulus intensity (C74) is reasonable given the lack of altered latencies. This addresses the relationship to prior work on parvafoxPvalb and pain.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals in the rostral dlPAG induces bradycardia in a subset of mice (3/8) with rapid onset and offset kinetics, anatomical specificity, and increased heart rate variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 describe cardiovascular effects in only 3 of 8 mice with appropriate anatomical specificity and temporal characteristics. However, the authors explicitly state this is 'observational' with insufficient sample size for statistical conclusions. The anatomical specificity (C79-C81) and HRV changes (C82) are compelling, but the limited n and lack of statistical validation prevent full support.

results.result: Chemogenetic and optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ neurons produces a phenotype consistent with innate defensive behavior, including tachypnea, immobility, and bradycardia, mediated at least partly through projections to the dlPAG.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85, C143-C144 synthesize the main findings across experimental modalities. The convergence of chemogenetic (respiratory) and optogenetic (immobility, bradycardia) results supports the overall conclusion. The inference that effects are mediated through dlPAG projections (C85) is reasonable given the anatomical and functional data, though the chemogenetic approach lacks projection specificity.

results.result: The authors propose that Foxb1+ and Cck+ neurons in the PMd represent distinct populations mediating opposite behaviors (immobility vs escape), potentially through differential targeting of GABAergic vs glutamatergic neurons in the dlPAG.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62, C104-C108, C111-C113, C145-C146 present a mechanistic hypothesis to reconcile opposing behavioral effects. While the scRNA-seq data (C112) supports distinct populations, the circuit mechanism (C107-C108, C111) remains speculative without direct evidence of differential connectivity to GABAergic interneurons. The hypothesis is plausible but requires validation through intersectional approaches or connectivity mapping.

results.result: The dlPAG receives multiple inputs including from Foxb1+ hypothalamic neurons, SF1+ VMH neurons, and glutamatergic superior colliculus neurons, all implicated in defensive behaviors with distinct functional properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C20 establish the broader circuit context through citations to established literature. These provide important background for interpreting the current findings but represent prior work rather than new results. The citations are appropriate and accurately represent the literature.

results.result: The authors propose downstream circuit mechanisms involving the cuneiform nucleus, vagal motor nuclei, and parasympathetic control to explain the respiratory and cardiovascular effects, supported by literature on dlPAG efferents and autonomic control.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88, C114-C126 propose circuit mechanisms based on literature citations. While the proposed pathways are anatomically plausible and supported by prior work, they remain speculative in the context of this study. The interpretation of HRV changes as parasympathetic (C124) is reasonable with appropriate citation, but direct circuit validation is lacking.

results.result: The authors discuss observations from unreported social interaction experiments and recent literature on social avoidance, suggesting that motor deficits may confound interpretation of social behaviors during Foxb1+ neuron activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 describe unreported observations that cannot be fully evaluated. Claims C130-C133 appropriately critique recent literature (Liu et al., 2022) by noting potential motor confounds, which is a valid concern given the immobility phenotype. However, without systematic data, this remains speculative. Claim C134 reasonably interprets the hot plate data.

results.result: The authors acknowledge technical limitations of optogenetic terminal stimulation including potential antidromic propagation and pH-mediated side effects of ArchT3.0, implementing appropriate experimental controls and stimulation paradigms.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136, C141-C142 demonstrate appropriate awareness of technical limitations with citations (Mahn et al., 2016, 2021; Rost et al., 2022). The use of intermittent stimulation for ArchT3.0 (C141) shows methodological sophistication. This transparency strengthens confidence in the results.

results.result: The authors provide extensive discussion of anatomical connectivity patterns and functional properties of PMd and parvafoxFoxb1 neurons based on prior literature, establishing the context for differential functional roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C103 synthesize prior anatomical and functional literature with appropriate citations. These establish important context for interpreting the current findings and support the hypothesis of distinct functional roles. The citations are accurate and comprehensive, though these represent background rather than new findings.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ hypothalamic neurons using hM3Dq led to increased respiratory effort, characterized by increased breaths per minute (BPM), minute volume, and peak inspiratory flow, while tidal volume remained unchanged. Control groups showed no significant respiratory changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes that 'the authors tend to attribute this effect to the activation of hM3Dq expressed in the parvofox Foxb1 but did not rule out the participation of the PMd Foxb1 cell group' due to the large viral injection volume. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'the observed effects on breathing are evident and dramatic' but notes the conclusion is 'not as strong as it could be.' The cellular source of the respiratory effect remains ambiguous.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Foxb1+ neurons produced minimal effects on gross locomotor activity, with only a small effect size on distance moved and no significant effect on time spent immobile.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes that 'the activation of the Foxb1hypothalamic cell groups in this experiment did not alter the gross locomotor activity, such as time spent immobile state. Thus, this contrasts with the authors' finding on the optogenetic activation.' This discrepancy between chemogenetic and optogenetic results raises questions about the interpretation of the locomotor findings.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals in the rostral dlPAG induced immobility and hypoactivity in mice, with effects being anatomically specific to the rostral dlPAG. Photoinhibition produced opposite effects, increasing locomotion and center time.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 confirms that 'optogenetic ChR2-mediated excitation of the Foxb1+ cell bodies' axonal endings in the dlPAG, leading to freezing' and notes 'the effective site to evoke freezing was the rostral PAGdl.' The editor describes these as 'solid studies' and reviewers accept the immobility findings, though Reviewer 1 suggests the effect likely arises from PMd Foxb1 rather than parvafox Foxb1 projections.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that their viral injection strategy led to ChR2 expression in both parvafoxFoxb1 and PMdFoxb1 neurons, though only PMd projects to the rostral dlPAG where optogenetic effects were observed.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly addresses this issue, noting 'the fibers projecting to the rostral PAGdl are likely to arise from the PMd Foxb1 cell group and not from the parvafox Foxb1 of the LHA.' The authors' acknowledgment of this technical limitation and the anatomical evidence supporting PMd as the source are accepted by reviewers.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis revealed that the PMd contains distinct subpopulations of Cck-expressing and Foxb1-expressing neurons, with substantial numbers of single-positive cells for each marker, supporting the existence of PMdFoxb1 as a novel functional subdivision.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges this finding, stating 'a specific population of PMd Foxb1 cells may be involved in producing freezing' in contrast to PMdCck cells that mediate escape. The scRNA-seq data demonstrating distinct Foxb1+ and Cck+ populations is not challenged by reviewers and supports the functional distinction between these populations.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Foxb1+ terminals in the rostral dlPAG induced bradycardia in a subset of mice (3 of 8), with rapid onset and offset kinetics and anatomical specificity to the rostral dlPAG.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'only a few of the animals with correct fiber placement presented sudden onset of bradycardia in response to the photostimulation,' highlighting the inconsistency of this effect. While the bradycardia data is acknowledged, the limited penetrance (3/8 mice) and lack of effect in control Pvalb-Cre mice raises questions about the robustness and generalizability of this finding.

results.result: Optogenetic manipulation of Foxb1+ neurons did not affect pain sensation in hot plate tests, and immobilized mice could still respond to nociceptive thermal stimuli.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges these findings. The hot plate results demonstrate that the immobility phenotype can be overcome by sufficiently strong stimuli, which is accepted as supporting evidence for the specificity of the behavioral effects.

results.result: The authors conclude that Foxb1+ hypothalamic neurons mediate a freezing-like defensive behavior characterized by tachypnea, immobility, and bradycardia, consistent with innate defensive responses.
results.evaluation: The editor states the findings are 'valuable' and 'solid studies,' but Reviewer 1 notes 'these findings are exciting, and, at this point, they need to be tested in a scenario of actual exposure to a natural predator.' Reviewer 3 states 'the conclusion is not as strong as it could be.' The overall interpretation is accepted as plausible but requires further validation in ethologically relevant contexts.

results.result: The authors propose that immobility could be mediated either by parvafoxFoxb1 terminals activating GABAergic interneurons in the dlPAG or by activation of Foxb1+/Cck- PMd neurons, representing distinct mechanisms from the escape-promoting PMdCck neurons.
results.evaluation: These are speculative mechanistic proposals acknowledged as such by the authors. Reviewer 1's comment that 'a specific population of PMd Foxb1 cells may be involved in producing freezing' supports the plausibility of the PMdFoxb1 hypothesis, but no reviewer provides explicit support for the GABAergic interneuron mechanism. These remain untested hypotheses.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate respiratory effects from chemogenetic activation (C21-C34). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED with comprehensive statistical evidence and appropriate controls. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN due to concerns about cellular source ambiguity - specifically whether effects arise from parvafox Foxb1 or PMd Foxb1 cells given large viral injection volume. Peer reviewers acknowledge effects are 'evident and dramatic' but question anatomical specificity.

Both address locomotor effects from chemogenetic activation (C35-C40). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED, noting small effect sizes appropriately distinguish respiratory from locomotor effects. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN and highlight a critical discrepancy: chemogenetic activation did NOT alter immobility, contrasting with optogenetic results that produced freezing. This inconsistency raises interpretation questions.

Both evaluate optogenetic immobility/freezing findings (C41-C52, C58-C59). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED with strong quantitative evidence and large effect sizes. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, confirming 'solid studies' showing ChR2 stimulation of dlPAG projections produces freezing. However, peer reviewers suggest effect likely arises from PMd Foxb1 rather than parvafox Foxb1 projections. Both also address bidirectional control (C53, C60) with ArchT3.0.

Both address technical limitations regarding viral spread and projection source (C54-C57). Both rate claims SUPPORTED. OpenEval commends transparency in acknowledging limitations while noting anatomical evidence supports PMd as source. Peer reviewers explicitly agree that 'fibers projecting to the rostral PAGdl are likely to arise from the PMd Foxb1 cell group and not from the parvafox Foxb1 of the LHA.' Strong concordance on this limitation.

Both evaluate scRNA-seq analysis identifying distinct Foxb1+ and Cck+ populations (C63-C70, with peer also including C112). Both rate claims SUPPORTED. OpenEval finds computational analysis methodologically sound with proper validation. Peer reviewers acknowledge this supports functional distinction between populations, with Reviewer 1 stating 'a specific population of PMd Foxb1 cells may be involved in producing freezing' versus PMdCck escape responses.

Both evaluate hot plate nociception results (C72-C74). Both rate claims SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes no significant differences with appropriate statistics and reasonable interpretation that immobility can be escaped with sufficient stimulus. Peer reviewers accept findings without challenge, agreeing this demonstrates immobility phenotype specificity - it can be overcome by strong stimuli.

Both evaluate cardiovascular/bradycardia effects (C75-C82). Both rate claims UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes compelling anatomical specificity and temporal characteristics but acknowledges limited sample size (3/8 mice) and lack of statistical validation. Peer reviewers similarly highlight inconsistency, noting 'only a few of the animals with correct fiber placement presented sudden onset of bradycardia,' questioning robustness and generalizability.

Both evaluate overall synthesis and main conclusions (C83-C85, C143-C144). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on convergence across modalities and reasonable inference about dlPAG mediation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN - editor calls findings 'valuable' and 'solid studies' but Reviewer 1 notes need for testing with natural predators and Reviewer 3 states 'conclusion is not as strong as it could be.' Peer reviewers accept plausibility but require further validation.

OpenEval notes scRNA-seq supports distinct populations but circuit mechanism regarding GABAergic interneurons remains speculative without direct evidence. Peer reviewers acknowledge PMdFoxb1 hypothesis plausibility but provide no explicit support for GABAergic interneuron mechanism. Both agree these remain untested hypotheses requiring validation.
